name: Schiaparelli entry, descent and landing demonstrator module
headline: Europe's Mars test lander thought it had landed while still 3.7 km up, and fell
story: On 19 October 2016, Schiaparelli fell into the thin air above Meridiani Planum. It was Europe's test lander, released three days earlier by its mothership, the Trace Gas Orbiter, to rehearse an entry, descent and landing on Mars. Its heat shield came away as planned, and its parachute opened about 12 kilometers above the ground.

Then the module spun faster than expected, and for about one second its motion sensor was overloaded. Mixing that bad reading with radar data, the navigation software computed an altitude below ground level. Believing it had landed, Schiaparelli released its parachute, fired its braking thrusters for 3 seconds instead of 30, and switched on its surface systems. It was still about 3.7 kilometers up.

It fell freely and struck the plain at an estimated 540 km/h. A day later, NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed a fresh dark scar; closer views soon found the parachute, back shell and heat shield nearby. By 2019 much of the dark blast pattern had faded, leaving a small shallow crater and a few bright fragments on the plains of Meridiani.

facts.label: Launched
facts.value: 14 March 2016, with the Trace Gas Orbiter, on a Proton-M from Baikonur

facts.label: Parachute opened
facts.value: About 12 km up, at about 1,730 km/h

facts.label: Impact speed
facts.value: About 540 km/h (ESA estimate), after free fall from about 3.7 km

images.caption: Before and after: NASA's Context Camera saw the plain on 29 May and again on 20 October 2016, the day after the descent. A new dark spot marks the lander; a bright dot to the south, its parachute.
25 October 2016: HiRISE's first look. Three impact points lie within 1.5 km of each other: the lander, the parachute with its back shell, and the heat shield.
14 December 2019: three years on, the dark streaks have faded, perhaps under settling dust, and the small crater left by the lander stands out more clearly.
